activities.anchor: reveals itself as a spiral, not a stripe
activities.caption: bet first — the band across the sky
activities.name: mwBandPredict

config.q: Why does the Milky Way appear as a hazy band across dark skies?
choices: We live inside a flat disc, edge-on — a hundred billion stars smear into a stripe
The band is a nearby nebula
config.why: The band is an illusion of viewpoint: seen from outside — as we see Andromeda — the same structure reveals itself as a spiral, not a stripe.

activities.anchor: smaller galaxies the Milky Way is still digesting
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the 21 cm trick
activities.name: mw21cmCloze

config.text: Optical astronomy cannot map our galaxy's structure because %%0%% blocks visible light. The %%1%% cm line of %%2%% sails through dust untouched — and its Doppler shift traced the spiral arms, revealing a barred spiral with the Sun on the Orion Spur.
config.hint: Predicted 1944, detected 1951 — and Gaia has since measured nearly two billion stars.

activities.anchor: That is where the trouble starts
activities.caption: place the Sun's galactic orbital speed
activities.name: mwSpeedPlace

config.prompt: The Sun orbits the galaxy's centre. Place its speed on the scale (km/s):
config.why: 230 km/s — and clouds far beyond the visible disc orbit at essentially the same speed: the flat rotation curve no visible mass can explain.
config.context: If the galaxy's mass were confined to its light, outer clouds should orbit slower — as Pluto orbits slower than Earth.

activities.anchor: mostly an invisible scaffolding that the stars happen to illuminate
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the missing share
activities.name: mwDarkEstimate

config.prompt: Dark matter outweighs ordinary matter roughly five to one. Roughly what per cent of the universe's matter is dark?
config.why: 5-to-1 means 5/6 ≈ 83% dark — 'an anomaly repeated across a hundred billion galaxies is a census of the universe's contents, and it comes out roughly 85% missing.'
config.context: Zwicky spotted the same discrepancy in clusters in 1933; Rubin's rotation curves made it unignorable in the 1970s.

activities.anchor: fails the old laws in exactly the way every other spiral galaxy does
activities.caption: rebuild the clean measurement — nothing exotic in it
activities.name: mwCleanOrder

config.prompt: The measurement that changed cosmology, step by step:
items: A cloud's radial speed comes from the Doppler shift of its 21 cm line
Its distance from the centre follows from simple geometry and a rotation model
The numbers test a centuries-old prediction — Kepler's and Newton's orbit laws
The laws fail — and every other spiral galaxy measured since fails the same way
config.why: The Milky Way is the only galaxy whose internal motions we can measure star by star — and it fails the old laws exactly like the rest.

activities.anchor: never been detected in a laboratory
activities.caption: true or false — what dark matter is not
activities.name: mwDarkJudge

statements.s: Dark matter is just cold gas, dead stars and planets — the MACHOs.
statements.why: Astronomers have accounted for all of those; they fall short by a factor of several.

statements.s: Dark matter interacts gravitationally — that is how we know it exists.
statements.why: It must, since gravity is the only evidence — but its particle nature is unknown.

statements.s: Dark matter outweighs ordinary matter roughly five to one.
statements.why: Your galaxy is mostly an invisible scaffolding the stars happen to illuminate.

statements.s: Dark matter is transparent to light of every wavelength.
statements.why: Which rules out ordinary matter entirely — and points to something never detected in a laboratory.

activities.caption: pair each neighbour with its relationship
activities.name: mwNeighbourMatch

pairs.right: 2.5 million light years away — the most distant naked-eye object, approaching at 110 km/s
our largest satellites, tidally stretched, gas feeding us for billions of years
dwarf galaxies barely brighter than a globular cluster — the statistical rule

config.why: In about 4.5 billion years Andromeda and the Milky Way braid into a single elliptical — stars almost never collide at these densities, but the merger is on the books.

activities.caption: pair each lunar feature with what it really is
activities.name: mnFeatureMatch

config.prompt: The Moon's face is a two-terrain map — match feature to identity:

pairs.right: the original crust — anorthosite, 4 billion years of impacts
giant impact basins flooded by basalt lava — about 16% of the surface, mostly near side

pairs.left: bright rays around craters like Tycho
pairs.right: ejecta splashed across the surface, fading with age — a crude clock
the day–night line where low sunlight casts the shadows that show relief

config.why: The far side, first photographed by Luna 3 in 1959, is almost all highlands — pocked and pale.

activities.anchor: gets exactly the same sunlight, only unseen from Earth
activities.caption: bet first — the far side's day
activities.name: mnFarPredict

config.q: Does the far side of the Moon ever receive sunlight?
choices: Yes, equally — it is the FAR side, not a dark one
config.why: Tidal locking hides the far side from Earth, not from the Sun: 'the dark side' does not exist.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — locking, libration and the slowing day
activities.name: mnLockCloze

config.text: The Moon's rotation period equals its orbital period — %%0%% days — and libration (±8° longitude, ±6.7° latitude) lets us see %%1%% per cent of the surface over time. Meanwhile Earth's day lengthens about %%2%% milliseconds per century.
config.hint: Locking is inevitable; the wobble is instructive; the brake still runs.

activities.caption: place the Moon's distance in Earth diameters
activities.name: mnDistancePlace

config.prompt: The Moon sits 384,400 km away — how many Earth diameters is that? Place it on the scale:
config.why: 30 Earth diameters — mostly empty space, and the cosmic coincidence (both ratio ≈ 400 and 390) that lets the Moon cover the Sun exactly.
config.context: No other planet enjoys both a large Moon and a near-perfect size-to-distance match — total eclipses are ours alone.

activities.anchor: so it lags outward relative to the planet's centre
activities.caption: file the tide facts — spring or neap?
activities.name: mnTideBuckets

config.prompt: The Sun contributes a pull about 46% as strong as the Moon's. File each arrangement:

items.label: Sun and Moon pulling in a line — their bulges add
Sun and Moon pulling at right angles — partial cancellation

config.why: The rhythm runs on a 14.8-day beat, and the two components (12.42 vs 12.00 hours) make the tide curve beat in and out over the day.

activities.caption: call the gap — the next pole star
activities.name: mnPoleEstimate

config.prompt: Earth's axis precesses once every 25,772 years. Roughly how many years until Vega becomes the pole star instead of Polaris?
config.why: About 12,000 years — halfway round the 25,772-year circle — and Thuban, the pole star when Egyptians built the pyramids, gets another turn.
config.context: Precession also shifts the equinoxes ~50 arcseconds per year, which is why star signs no longer match the Sun's constellation.

activities.anchor: a Theia surprisingly similar to Earth
activities.caption: pair each origin hypothesis with why it fails
activities.name: mnOriginMatch

config.prompt: The Giant Impact Hypothesis earns its status by passing tests its rivals fail:

pairs.right: the Moon's low iron vs Earth's iron-rich core doesn't match two siblings
no plausible trajectory slows it without extravagant energy
the system's angular momentum is far too small
iron sank with Theia's core, mantle debris made the Moon, simulations match

config.why: One residue keeps research honest: Earth and Moon rocks have nearly identical oxygen isotopes — solved with a hot, well-mixed post-impact Earth.
